title: Running through August 30th at SoHo Playhouse in NYC, via Black Watch...
transcript: What if all men on earth suddenly ☠️ and women built a new society from scratch? That's the question in this new play, Hungry Women by Melissa Maney, starring Tony nominee Julia Lester. Starting off in the late 1800s, the play is told in three acts, each jumping forward a century to see how society progresses. And each actor plays loose variations of the same figure throughout. So in particular, there's always one woman who is trying to maintain the status quo for her own benefit, and one who is always questioning and transgressing against it. The tone ranges from heightened satire to earnest parable, and meanwhile, some shockingly dark and gruesome things take place. That made me go, “oh, wow, okay! we're doing *that*? But the slight tonal whiplash ended up feeling justified by the insightful concept that encompassed. I had one of the most intriguing post show conversations I've had in a while as my friend and I discussed the surprisingly twisty implications of where the story goes. It's not the straightforward middle finger to the patriarchy that it might present itself as at first. Not that it pulls any punches in showing how poorly women have been treated throughout history, but it goes on to raise some larger and more challenging questions to ponder as you leave the theater about power and human civilization as a whole. Even just the fact that men disappear in the late 1800s specifically inspires some thought provoking contrast about what this Society would look like with *that* as their starting point and not 2026
